text: Does the pain feel localized to the inside of your knee, and do you experience any instability or a sensation of the knee "giving way"?

speaker: Doctor
text: The location of your pain, specifically on the medial aspect of the tibia just below the kneecap, combined with your history of recent increased activity, suggests a stress reaction or fracture. text: RESULTS: X-Ray_Knee Findings: No fracture, dislocation, or appreciable joint effusion.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the negative X-ray and your history of repetitive pivoting and increased activity, I suspect patellofemoral pain syndrome or patellar tendinopathy. Do you experience pain specifically when kneeling, squatting, or climbing stairs?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), currently managed with oral contraceptive pills. Social history: Has recently joined a volleyball team.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see. Do you have any point tenderness directly over the patellar tendon, or is the pain more diffuse around the kneecap?

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the pain is located on the medial aspect of the tibia rather than the patellar tendon, and you have no swelling or acute injury, this presentation is classic for medial tibial stress syndrome, commonly known as shin splints. Do you feel a dull ache along the inner edge of your shin bone that worsens with activity?

speaker: Patient

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the negative X-ray and the specific location of pain on the medial tibial plateau with a history of pivoting sports, I am concerned for a medial meniscus tear which may not be visible on plain film. I will request an MRI to visualize the soft tissues. REQUEST TEST: Knee_MRI

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal MRI rules out a meniscal tear, leaving us with a soft tissue issue likely related to your recent increase in volleyball activity. Do you experience pain specifically when descending stairs or after sitting for long periods with your knees bent?

speaker: Patient

speaker: Doctor
text:
The repeated denial of swelling or acute injury, combined with normal imaging, points toward an overuse injury like patellofemoral pain syndrome rather than a structural tear. I have enough information to form a conclusion based on the clinical history and exclusion of other causes.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
